questions.question: A PM hands over "look into the activation drop and come back with what you find." The delegate returns competent work answering a different question. What failed?
options: The delegate lacked the judgment to identify the decision behind the request
The intent was not portable — the decision the work serves, and its alternatives, stayed in the PM's head
The time box was too short for a proper investigation
The PM should have reviewed progress at the halfway point
questions.explanation: A topic was handed over, not a decision, so the delegate had nothing to optimise against but the task. Option D is the tempting fix a PM reaches for after one bad handover — a mid-point check would have caught the drift, but it treats a missing contract as a monitoring problem and keeps the PM as the constraint.

questions.question: A PM writes a detailed contract for the activation investigation, then adds: "You own this now." What is wrong with that last sentence?
options: Nothing — clear ownership is what makes delegation work
It should specify which parts they own and which the PM retains
It conflicts with the escalation conditions, which imply the PM is still involved
Accountability for the outcome does not transfer with the work, and saying it does pushes the delegate to over-hedge or over-commit
questions.explanation: Delegation moves the work and sometimes the choice; it never moves the consequence out of your area. Option A is the standard management instinct and it sounds empowering, but a delegate who believes they now carry the consequence will manage their own risk instead of the decision's.

questions.question: An associate PM is ready to grow. The work is a reversible copy experiment on the empty document state. What does the boundary of this lesson recommend?
options: Delegate the framing, leave the frame deliberately open, and say that the ambiguity is the assignment
Write a full five-element contract, since consistent contracts build good habits
Delegate at the execute level first, then raise the level once they have delivered
Keep the framing and delegate the analysis, so the learning is contained
questions.explanation: Framing is how judgment develops, and low-consequence reversible work is where it is safe to develop it. Option B is the trained answer — a complete contract handed to someone ready to frame the problem converts growth work into execution work while the PM tells themselves they are developing someone.

questions.question: Which of these is usable as an escalation condition in a delegation contract?
options: "Come back if you feel the investigation is going off track."
"Escalate anything that might affect the enterprise accounts."
"Come back before continuing if the decline concentrates in one acquisition channel."
"Check in with me weekly so we can review progress together."
questions.explanation: An escalation condition must be an observation the delegate can actually see with the access you gave them. Option B is the tempting one: it names something consequential, but "might affect" is a judgment call, so the delegate either escalates constantly or waits until it is obvious, which is too late.

questions.question: A PM's contract for the activation work is silent on whether the inherited activation definition can be challenged. Why does that single omission matter so much?
options: It leaves the delegate unsure who to ask, which will cost a few days
It affects whether the analysis is comparable with historical reporting
It decides whether the assignment is measuring a decline or questioning whether the measure describes the job at all
It means the evidence standard cannot be applied, since the metric is undefined
questions.explanation: Those are two different assignments with different outputs, and the delegate will assume the narrower one. Option D is close and reads well, but the standard can be applied to the inherited definition perfectly well — the problem is that doing so answers a question the PM may not have meant to ask.
